title: Clairaut's Theorem: Order Doesn't Matter
topic: Clairaut's (Schwarz's) theorem for smooth functions: ∂²f/∂x∂y = ∂²f/∂y∂x. The two computation paths — differentiate x then y, or y then x — converge to the same expression. The geometric reading: take a small rectangle of side h × k, the corner-sum (f(x+h,y+k) − f(x,y+k) − f(x+h,y) + f(x,y))/(h·k) approaches the mixed partial from both sides as the rectangle shrinks.

beats.narration: Mixed partials: differentiate in x, then in y. Or do it the other way round. The order should not matter — and for smooth functions, it doesn't.

elements.content: x then y, or y then x — same answer.

beats.narration: Pick a function: f equals x squared y, plus sine of x y. Walk the left path: differentiate in x first, then in y. Walk the right path: differentiate in y first, then in x. Two different intermediate expressions, but the second derivative lands on the same place.

Why does this happen? Take a tiny rectangle of width h and height k anchored at the point. Add the corners of f with alternating signs and divide by h k. As the rectangle shrinks, the two ways to slice it — rows first or columns first — give the same limit. That limit is the mixed partial.

elements.content: An x–y grid with a small rectangle h × k at the chosen point (GENUINE MORPHING MOTION as the rectangle shrinks)
Corner values f(x,y), f(x+h,y), f(x,y+k), f(x+h,y+k) labelled with + and − signs
Live readout of the corner-sum approximation to f_xy as the rectangle shrinks

beats.narration: The theorem needs a continuity condition. If both mixed partials exist and are continuous, they agree. For polynomials, exponentials, sines, and almost everything you meet in this course, that holds.

elements.content: If f_xy and f_yx are continuous near (a, b), then f_xy(a, b) = f_yx(a, b).
Holds for every smooth function in this course.

beats.narration: Mixed partials commute. The Hessian matrix is symmetric.
